title: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Short programs in ordinary low-level languages can behave randomly

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Because register machines idealize programs in low-level languages such as C, Basic, Java or assembler, searching many millions of short programs in such languages typically yields at least a few with complex, seemingly random behavior.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. 3: The World of Simple Programs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: searching through many millions of short programs typically yields at least a few that exhibit complex and seemingly random behavior.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 3, “The World of Simple Programs”; section “Symbolic Systems” (from p. 102), p. 102. Scope: short programs in practical low-level programming languages

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch03-16: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.70

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Program generation and execution are straightforward, and a broad corpus of public code exists. But finite searches and chosen randomness tests resolve only specified languages, length bounds, inputs, and runtimes, not the unrestricted wording.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fix language grammars, program-length bounds, inputs, runtimes, and statistical or compression-based complexity criteria, then exhaustively sample or enumerate programs. Finding qualifying programs in most sampled languages supports the claim; finding none under generous bounds weakens it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The meanings of short, typically, and seemingly random require contestable thresholds.

The named practical languages are only loosely idealized by register machines.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.65
data adequacy: 0.55
data existence: 0.85
operationalizability: 0.65
analysis feasibility: 0.8

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The search Wolfram describes is a finite enumeration that public compilers can repeat, and a handful of complex-looking outputs would support the claim as an existence result. 'Complex and seemingly random' and 'typically' across practical languages still need a chosen battery of tests and a chosen notion of program length, so the replication tests a proxy for the full wording. A small team can run that proxy in weeks, but the result would not cleanly cover every low-level language.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Enumerate millions of short programs in one or two low-level languages, run each for a fixed number of steps, and apply compression and statistical randomness tests to the output. Finding a few outputs that pass those tests confirms the existential part; finding none in a large bounded search would challenge 'typically.'

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
What counts as a short program depends on the language's syntax, so the same behavior can look rare or common under a different encoding.

Statistical tests can fail to detect hidden regularity, and they do not prove that an output is random.
